title: are Sikhs Hindu or Muslim?
hook: the question Sikhs get asked from both sides, and the plain answer: a learner, on a path of its own
carry: a learner, on a path of its own

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ardas, the standing prayer that ends with the good of all. Today, a question many Sikhs get asked, and a plain answer to it.

So, are Sikhs a kind of Hindu? Or a kind of Muslim? Sikhs hear both, sometimes in the same week. Surveys in the United States have found many people guessing Sikhism is a branch of Islam; others assume it's part of Hinduism. The plain answer is neither. And why people mix it up turns out to be a good story.
screen: `A KIND OF HINDU?` → `A KIND OF MUSLIM?` → `THE PLAIN ANSWER: NEITHER.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Sikh is Punjabi for a learner, a student: someone who learns from the Guru. So nobody starts out finished. The path began with Guru Nanak, born, tradition says, in 1469, in Punjab, and grew through ten Gurus over about two hundred years. It has its own scripture, its own initiation, which you met on day four, and its own houses of worship. So it's a religion of its own, not a branch of another. Why the mix-up? Nanak was born into a Hindu family and grew up among Hindu and Muslim neighbors. His companion on years of travel, Mardana, was a Muslim musician. Sikh scripture uses names for God that both neighbors used, and it even holds hymns by holy poets born into Hindu and Muslim families, beside the Gurus' own. Sharing words isn't the same as being the same. Then there's the turban and the beard, which people who don't know often read as Muslim, and that mistake hasn't always been harmless. The first words Nanak is remembered saying, as his mission began, were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Some hear in that: beneath the labels, everyone is made by the one. Others hear a challenge: nobody was living up to the name they carried. Either way, it put no one down. It was a starting point.
screen: `SIKH — A LEARNER.` · `ITS OWN PATH, FROM GURU NANAK.` · `SHARING WORDS ISN'T BEING THE SAME.` · `THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, notice one label people put on you. On the second, notice one you put on someone else. On the third, set both down for a breath, and see the person underneath.
Sikh. A learner, a student of the Guru, on a path that began with Guru Nanak. Sixth word.
Your line: a learner, on a path of its own. That's the plain answer, and it needs nobody else's faith put down to say it. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: a learner, a disciple; from the Sanskrit shishya, a student.

trapdoor: what you thought: just the name of the religion.
what it means: a learner, a student of the Guru, on a path of its own that began with Guru Nanak.

what a scholar hears: sikh comes from the Sanskrit shishya, disciple. Nanak's words, there is no Hindu, there is no Musalman, come from the janamsakhis, the life-stories, and are read in more than one way.

story.title: the thread that wouldn't break
story.text: A boy of about eleven sits in front of the family priest, guests all around, on the day he's meant to receive a sacred cotton thread over his shoulder. The priest reaches for it, and the boy asks: what is this for, and will it last? He isn't mocking anyone. He says he'd gladly wear a thread spun from compassion and contentment, knotted with self-control and twisted with truth: one that never breaks, never gets dirty, never burns and is never lost. The boy was Nanak.
story.source: janamsakhi tradition; the hymn of the thread is in Asa di Var (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471)

wrong.myth: Sikhism is a mix of Hinduism and Islam.
wrong.truth: it grew among Hindu and Muslim neighbors and shares some words with both, but it's a path of its own, with its own Gurus, scripture and practice.

Hook: 'Surveys in the United States have found many people guessing Sikhism is a branch of Islam' rests on the ABA article's citation of a 2013 survey (49% of Americans believed Sikhism was a sect of Islam). The number is deliberately not spoken. Confirm.
Misidentification: 'that mistake hasn't always been harmless' is the only reference to post-2001 hate crimes, kept gentle for week one. The Balbir Singh Sodhi story is on day 320. Confirm.
'Grew through ten Gurus over about two hundred years' (Guru Nanak's mission c. 1499 to Guru Gobind Singh's death in 1708). Confirm.
